text: The map sends x∈A to the character h↦b(x,h) on H, with values in the additive group ℚ/ℤ. Biadditivity makes this a character and makes the assignment additive in x. This is restriction of the adjoint pairing used in [Nikulin’s finite discriminant forms, §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677); no nondegeneracy is required to define it. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L78) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L84) passes.
Evaluation is exactly the original pairing on a subgroup element.
Its kernel is exactly H⊥.

Evaluating the character assigned to x at h∈H gives b(x,h), with h viewed in A. This is the defining evaluation formula for the restricted adjoint in [Nikulin’s finite discriminant forms, §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677), so it introduces no rescaling or different pairing. Membership in H is already supplied by the input’s subtype. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L84) passes.
The evaluation convention yields exactly the expected orthogonal-complement kernel.

The restricted adjoint vanishes on x exactly when b(x,h)=0 for every h∈H. Its kernel is therefore H⊥, matching the orthogonality convention of [Nikulin’s finite discriminant forms, §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677). Here zero means the zero ℚ/ℤ-valued character, not merely a character with some zero value. Degenerate pairings are allowed. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L107) passes.
The cardinality proof uses this exact kernel together with separately assumed perfectness.

Every ℚ/ℤ-valued character of H extends to A by [character extension](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Module/CharacterModule.lean#L101). The nondegeneracy hypothesis says the adjoint A→Hom(A,ℚ/ℤ) is bijective, so that extension is pairing with some x∈A. Restricting back gives the desired character. The hypothesis is essential: a zero pairing cannot represent nonzero characters. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L107) passes.
Surjectivity identifies the image with the full character group when computing the index.

The restricted pairing maps A onto the characters of H, with kernel H⊥; [character extension](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Module/CharacterModule.lean#L101) and perfectness supply surjectivity. Since a finite abelian group has as many ℚ/ℤ-valued characters as elements, the kernel-index formula gives |H|·|H⊥|=|A|. Nat.card is an actual finite count here, and no isotropy is needed. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L134) passes.
The native double-complement proof uses the cardinality identity twice.

For a perfect finite pairing, H lies in H⊥⊥ and the cardinality formula gives both subgroups the same order, hence equality. This is the finite nondegenerate orthogonality of [Nikulin’s finite discriminant forms, §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677). The explicit perfectness hypothesis excludes the degenerate case, where the double complement instead enlarges H by the radical. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L192) passes.
The general theorem recovers the degenerate case by passing through the nondegenerate radical quotient.

Write π:A→A/rad(b). The statement is π(H)⊥=π(H⊥): every quotient element has a representative, and the descended pairing on representatives is b. Thus testing orthogonality to π(H) is exactly testing against H. This uses [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28); π need not be injective and H need not contain the radical. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L192) passes.
The general double-complement proof uses this transport through the radical quotient.

For a possibly degenerate finite pairing, H⊥⊥ is H+rad(b), where the displayed subgroup supremum means the subgroup sum. Quotienting out the radical gives the perfect finite pairing of [Nikulin’s finite discriminant forms, §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677); double complementation there recovers H’s image, whose preimage is H+rad(b). This explains the necessary correction to H alone. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L232) passes.
The radical of the restricted pairing uses this precise subgroup sum.

Here a bilinear Lagrangian means H=H⊥. Perfectness gives |H|·|H⊥|=|A|, so replacing H⊥ by H yields |H|²=|A|, as in [Nikulin’s finite discriminant forms, §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677). Both hypotheses are explicit. Nat.card counts finite groups, and this bilinear result makes no assertion that a quadratic refinement vanishes on H. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Metabolic.lean#L37) passes.
The quadratic consumer first forgets a supplied quadratic Lagrangian to its bilinear condition and retains perfectness.

A vector in H⊥ is radical for the restricted pairing exactly when it also lies in H⊥⊥=H+rad(b). The right side therefore means (H+rad(b))∩H⊥, viewed inside H⊥. This combines the orthogonality convention of [Nikulin’s finite discriminant forms, §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677) with the general double-complement formula; no nondegeneracy or isotropy is silently assumed. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Quotient.lean#L188) passes.
The orthogonal quotient’s nondegeneracy criterion uses exactly this restricted radical.

An element h of H∩H⊥ pairs to zero with every x∈H⊥, because b(h,x)=b(x,h)=0. Thus this intersection lies in the radical of b restricted to H⊥, permitting [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28). The claim holds for every H; writing all of H inside H⊥ would require isotropy. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Quotient.lean#L110) passes.
The quotient enabled by this inclusion evaluates to b on representatives.

This construction is H⊥/(H∩H⊥), with pairing induced from b. Every element divided out pairs trivially with H⊥, so [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28) makes the value independent of representatives. No isotropy is required for this general construction. If H is bilinearly isotropic, H≤H⊥ and it becomes the usual quotient H⊥/H. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Quotient.lean#L110) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Quotient.lean#L144) passes.
The induced pairing agrees with b on representatives.
The quotient map kills exactly H∩H⊥ inside H⊥.

The quotient H⊥/(H∩H⊥) is perfect exactly when rad(b)≤H. Indeed the restricted radical is (H+rad(b))∩H⊥; the quotient removes precisely H∩H⊥, while rad(b) already lies in H⊥. This extends [Nikulin’s orthogonal reduction, §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677) to arbitrary H and degenerate ambient pairings, with the residual radical explicitly accounted for. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Quotient.lean#L206) passes.
The ambient-perfect specialization sets rad(b)=0 and satisfies the precise containment criterion.

The quotient’s order is the index of H∩H⊥ as a subgroup of H⊥, directly from its [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61). The index is not taken in the whole ambient group A. All groups are finite, so Nat.card and subgroup index are ordinary finite counts; neither nondegeneracy nor isotropy is required. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Quotient.lean#L220) passes.
The general nondegenerate order formula uses this index in H⊥.

Perfectness gives |H⊥|·|H|=|A|, while [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61) give |H⊥/(H∩H⊥)|·|H∩H⊥|=|H⊥|. Multiplying yields exactly the stated three-factor formula. The intersection factor is necessary for an arbitrary subgroup H; isotropy is not assumed. Nat.card denotes actual finite orders, and the multiplicative form avoids any division convention. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Quotient.lean#L231) passes.
Under isotropy the intersection is all of H, yielding the squared-order specialization.

Bilinear isotropy supplies H≤H⊥, so H∩H⊥ is all of H. In the perfect ambient pairing, the general order formula therefore becomes |H⊥/H|·|H|²=|A|, matching [Nikulin’s orthogonal reduction, §1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677). Nat.card is ordinary finite cardinality. This concerns the bilinear quotient; descending a quadratic refinement would additionally require q|H=0. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L1048) passes.
The quadratic specialization explicitly supplies quadratic isotropy, hence the required bilinear isotropy.

The two hypotheses say q vanishes on K and every k∈K pairs trivially with all of A. These are exactly the two conditions in [quadratic radical](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/QuadraticForm/Radical.lean#L35); together they give q(x+k)=q(x). Merely having b vanish on K×K would not suffice for a quotient of all A, so the ambient-radical hypothesis matters. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L874) passes.
The orthogonal-quotient construction supplies both conditions after restricting to H⊥.

The carrier is the additive group A/K, implemented as the ℤ-module quotient by K with its existing subgroup elements. This is precisely the group of [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61); no pairing is part of this abbreviation. Consequently it is defined for every subgroup K, while descending b requires the later radical-containment hypothesis. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L191) passes.
When the pairing descends, the carrier’s order is exactly the subgroup index.

If K lies in rad(b), every k∈K has b(k,y)=0 for all y. Thus K, viewed as the same subgroup with ℤ-module structure, lies in the kernel of the linear map k↦b(k,−). This is the annihilation condition needed by [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28), not merely vanishing of self-pairings. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L82) passes.
The descended bilinear map evaluates to the original pairing on representatives.

The value at ([x],[y]) is b(x,y) in ℚ/ℤ. Because K lies in the radical, replacing either representative by an element differing by K adds zero to the value. Symmetry handles both arguments of [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28). The construction retains ℤ-bilinearity and does not assume the induced pairing is nondegenerate. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L82) passes.
The lift has the exact representative evaluation formula.

Evaluating the descended ℤ-bilinear map on [x] and [y] returns b(x,y), exactly the computation rule for [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28). The hypothesis K≤rad(b) ensures this remains unchanged if either representative is altered by K. The formula concerns all x,y∈A and requires no nondegeneracy or quadratic refinement. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L126) passes.
The packaged finite bilinear module preserves this same evaluation rule.

This additive map is the canonical projection x↦[x] from A onto A/K, using [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61). The radical hypothesis equips the target with the descended pairing; it does not alter the quotient map. Its kernel is exactly K, so it is generally not an embedding even though it preserves pairing values. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L141) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L136) passes.
Its kernel is exactly K.
Every quotient class has a representative.

The packaged quotient pairing satisfies b̄([x],[y])=b(x,y), matching [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28). This identifies the actual stored pairing, not just an abstractly isometric form. Radical containment ensures independence of both representatives; the result remains valid when the ambient pairing and the quotient pairing are degenerate. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L161) passes.
The radical-image proof tests quotient orthogonality using this representative formula.

Every element of A/K has a representative x∈A, as for [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61); hence the canonical map is surjective. Radical containment is needed for the target’s pairing, not for this elementary property of the underlying quotient group. No distinguished representative or injective section is asserted. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L161) passes.
The radical comparison uses surjectivity to test against every quotient element through representatives.

The kernel of x↦[x] is exactly the subgroup K, as for [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61). Converting K to a ℤ-submodule and back preserves its elements, so the result is an equality of additive subgroups of A. Radical containment ensures the pairing descends but does not enlarge the kernel to all of rad(b). Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L148) passes.
The kernel equality yields the exact zero-class membership criterion.

The class of x is zero exactly when x belongs to K, the zero-class rule for [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61). Although K must lie in rad(b) to define the quotient pairing, a radical element outside K need not have zero class. This distinction is essential when identifying degeneracy that remains in the quotient. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L154) passes.
The zero criterion gives equality of classes exactly when their difference lies in K.

The radical of the quotient pairing is the image of rad(b) under A→A/K. By [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28), [x] pairs trivially with every [y] exactly when x pairs trivially with every y. Surjectivity supplies all quotient elements. Thus quotienting a subgroup of the radical creates no additional radical classes. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L179) passes.
The quotient is perfect exactly when the radical image becomes zero.

The quotient pairing is perfect exactly when rad(b)≤K. Its radical is the image of rad(b), which vanishes precisely when those elements lie in the quotient kernel K. Since K≤rad(b) is already assumed, this means K=rad(b). This is the canonical radical removal underlying [Nikulin’s finite discriminant forms, §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677), extended to arbitrary such K. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L235) passes.
Taking K to be the whole radical produces the expected perfect quotient.

The quotient group A/K has |A/K|=[A:K], directly from [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61) and the projection’s kernel K. Nat.card and index here count finite groups, because finiteness is part of A’s structure. The result does not require a perfect pairing: radical containment is used only to equip the quotient with its pairing. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Quotient.lean#L213) passes.
Restricting to H⊥ specializes this count to the orthogonal quotient’s correct subgroup index.

This is A/rad(b) with pairing b̄([x],[y])=b(x,y), formed by [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28). Radical elements pair to zero with everything, so both representatives may be changed without altering the value. Dividing out the entire radical removes exactly the remaining degeneracy; this construction concerns the bilinear pairing and does not presume a quadratic refinement descends. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L212) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L235) passes.
Its pairing has the exact representative value.
The resulting finite pairing is perfect.

The map sends x to its class modulo rad(b), using [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61). It is an additive surjection whose kernel is the radical; it can identify distinct elements in a degenerate module. The descended pairing remains equal to b on representatives, so this canonical projection preserves pairing values without necessarily being an isometry equivalence. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L223) passes, Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/RadicalQuotient.lean#L219) passes.
The kernel is precisely rad(b).
Every radical-quotient element has a representative.

The pairing of [x] and [y] modulo rad(b) equals b(x,y), the representative rule of [bilinear descent](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Bilinear.lean#L28). Changing either representative adds a radical element and contributes zero. The statement identifies the stored quotient pairing exactly, so it supports subsequent transport of orthogonality without choosing representatives or rescaling the form. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L168) passes.
Orthogonal complements commute with the radical projection using this evaluation rule.

Every class modulo rad(b) is represented by some x∈A, so the canonical radical projection is onto, as for [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61). This does not imply the original pairing was perfect or that the projection is injective; its kernel is the entire original radical. No particular representative is selected by the assertion. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L168) passes.
Orthogonality transport begins by choosing a representative via this surjectivity.

An element maps to zero modulo rad(b) exactly when it lies in rad(b), so the kernel is the radical itself. This is the kernel formula for [quotient classes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/Defs.lean#L61), specialized to the chosen subgroup. It explains why pulling a subgroup’s image back along the projection enlarges that subgroup by rad(b). Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L192) passes.
The general double-complement proof uses this kernel to recover H+rad(b).

After quotienting by rad(b), the induced pairing has zero radical: a class annihilating every class has a representative already in rad(b), hence is zero. For finite groups this makes the adjoint bijective, the perfectness convention of [Nikulin’s finite discriminant forms, §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677). The claim is bilinear; it does not assert descent of an arbitrary quadratic refinement. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Orthogonal/Complement.lean#L192) passes.
The general double-complement theorem applies the perfect-case theorem to this radical quotient.

A homeomorphism restricts to the sets selected by two predicates when membership corresponds in both directions. The forward map is the original homeomorphism and the inverse is its restriction. Both sets carry their inherited topologies, so continuity follows by restriction and viewing the codomain as a subspace. [Semmes Def.2.8.2; Props.2.8.4–5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Lemmas.lean#L160).

A subset is homeomorphic to its image under a homeomorphism, using the original map and its inverse restricted to those sets. The subset and image are spaces with their inherited topologies. Their ambient openness or closedness is unnecessary: continuity of restrictions and maps into subspaces supplies both directions. [Semmes Def.2.8.2; Props.2.8.4–5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Lemmas.lean#L344).

An embedding identifies the inverse image of a subset of its range with that subset itself. The range-containment hypothesis makes the restricted map surjective; injectivity and the inherited topologies make it a homeomorphism. The displayed map is the original embedding restricted to the inverse image, even for an empty subset. [Semmes Def.2.8.2; Props.2.8.4–5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Lemmas.lean#L432).

An embedding is a homeomorphism from its domain onto its range equipped with the subspace topology. This construction keeps the original forward map and uses its unique preimage as inverse. Surjectivity onto the ambient target is unnecessary; the range restriction supplies exactly the bijection needed for the standard homeomorphism definition. [Semmes Def.2.8.2; Prop.2.8.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Lemmas.lean#L411).

A surjective embedding gives a homeomorphism between the entire source and target. Embedding supplies injectivity and the correct inherited topology, while surjectivity supplies every inverse value. The construction retains the original forward map; its inverse is continuous because the embedding identifies the source topology with the topology pulled back from the target. [Semmes Def.2.8.2; Prop.2.8.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Lemmas.lean#L423).

An open map sends every neighborhood of x to a neighborhood of its image. A neighborhood here may be larger than an open set: choose an open set containing x inside it, then take its open image. Neither continuity nor surjectivity is required for this forward neighborhood property. [Semmes Def.2.8.3; §1.7](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L389).

The range of an open map is open in the whole target, since it is the image of the entire source, an open set. This uses the standard image-of-open-sets definition directly. Continuity and surjectivity are unnecessary, and an empty source correctly gives the empty open range. [Semmes Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L385).

Composing two closed embeddings again identifies the source with a closed subspace of the final target. The inherited topology and injectivity compose, and the second closed embedding sends the first closed range to a closed set. Thus both the embedding condition and ambient closedness of the resulting range are retained. [Semmes §1.5.1; Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L863).

The composite of two embeddings is an embedding: injectivity composes, and pulling back the topology through the two maps equals pulling it back through their composite. This is the familiar fact that a subspace of a subspace has its inherited ambient topology. Neither image is required to be open or closed. [Semmes §1.5; Props.2.8.4–5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L213).

Give the domain exactly the topology pulled back along a map from its target. The map then induces that topology by construction. This topology is supplied implicitly in the displayed signature, rather than being an arbitrary preexisting topology. Injectivity is unnecessary; for an inclusion this is the usual subspace construction. [Semmes Def.1.5.1; Prop.1.5.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L63).

Two successive identifications with open subspaces compose to an identification with an open subspace of the final target. Injectivity and inherited topology compose, and openness follows because the second open embedding sends the first open range to an open set. No separation or nonemptiness assumptions are needed. [Semmes §1.5; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L780).

An embedding with open range sends open domain sets to open sets in the whole target. The embedding first makes their images relatively open in its range; the range itself being open makes them ambiently open. This explains why the open-range hypothesis supplies more than the ordinary subspace topology alone. [Semmes Def.1.5.1; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L712).

An embedding that is also an open map has open range, since the entire domain is open. It therefore identifies its domain with an open subspace of the target. Both assumptions retain their standard meanings: embedding includes injectivity and inherited topology, while openness concerns images of arbitrary open subsets. [Semmes Def.1.5.1; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L747).

If f is continuous and onto, and g after f is open, then g is open. For an open subset of the intermediate space, pull it back through f and apply openness of the composite. Surjectivity makes the resulting image exactly its image under g, as required. [Semmes Prop.2.7.9; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L380).

A space with at most one point has only one topology. Consequently every map from it induces its existing topology by pullback from the target. The assumption includes the empty space, not just a singleton. No separation property of the target or additional continuity hypothesis is needed for this conclusion. [Semmes §1.1; Def.1.5.1](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L175).

The composite of two quotient maps is a quotient map. It remains surjective, and a subset of the final target is open exactly when its successive inverse images are open. The two inverse-image criteria combine into the criterion for the composite, with no assumption that either map sends open sets to open sets. [Semmes §5.6.1, (5.6.5–6)](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L337).

A continuous retraction g with a continuous section f is a quotient map: g composed with f is the identity, so g is onto. If an inverse image under g is open, pulling it back by f recovers the original open set. Only this one-sided inverse identity is assumed. [Semmes §5.6.1; Prop.2.7.9](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L355).

Every embedding restricts to a homeomorphism between a subset of its domain and that subset’s image. Both are equipped with their inherited topologies; the map is the original embedding on the subset. Injectivity supplies a unique inverse there, so surjectivity onto the entire ambient target is unnecessary. [Semmes Def.2.8.2; Props.2.8.4–5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Lemmas.lean#L428).

The inverse image of a dense set under an open map is dense. Every nonempty open source set has a nonempty open image, which meets the dense target set; a preimage of that intersection lies in the original source set. Continuity and surjectivity are unnecessary, and the empty source is allowed. [Semmes Defs.1.3.1, 2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L531).

The composite g after f sends open sets to open sets when each map does. Its image of any set is the successive image under f and then g, so the two openness assumptions apply in order. Continuity, injectivity, and surjectivity are not part of this open-map statement. [Semmes Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L376).

When the source topology is pulled back along f, inverse images of a neighborhood basis at f(x) form a neighborhood basis at x. The same qualifying indices are retained. This extends the usual intersection formula for a subspace basis to possibly noninjective maps; basis members need not themselves be open. [Semmes Prop.1.7.13](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L94).

A map whose domain topology is exactly pulled back from its target is continuous: the inverse image of every open target set is open by construction. This is the same reason a subspace inclusion is continuous. The formal statement permits noninjective maps, with identified points topologically indistinguishable in the domain. [Semmes Prop.2.7.9; §2.7.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L134).

Suppose f induces the source topology and its range contains a neighborhood of f(x). Then g is continuous at f(x) exactly when g after f is continuous at x. The neighborhood assumption makes testing on the range sufficient locally; f need not be injective or globally surjective. [Semmes §2.7; Prop.2.8.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L129).

Continuity of g at a point in an open embedded copy can be tested after composing with that embedding. Its open range contains a full neighborhood of the image point, and its inherited topology preserves neighborhoods there. Thus the equivalence concerns ordinary ambient continuity at that point, without any global surjectivity assumption. [Semmes §2.7; Prop.2.8.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L734).

An open embedding transports the neighborhood filter at x to the full neighborhood filter at f(x). Embedding supplies the inherited topology, while open range ensures those relative neighborhoods are ambient neighborhoods. Equality concerns the filter generated by these images; it does not require every target neighborhood to equal an image. [Semmes §1.7; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L715).

A map induces the domain topology exactly when every neighborhood filter is the pullback of the neighborhood filter at its image point. Concretely, every source neighborhood contains the inverse image of some target neighborhood, and such inverse images are neighborhoods. This is the neighborhood form of inherited topology, allowing noninjective maps. [Semmes §1.5; Prop.1.7.13](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L86).

The composite of closed maps is closed because it takes a closed set first to a closed subset of the intermediate space and then to a closed subset of the target. The assertion concerns images of closed sets. It neither assumes nor concludes continuity, injectivity, or surjectivity of either map. [Semmes §1.4; Prop.2.7.9](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L546).

A closed map has closed range in its ambient target: apply the image-of-closed-sets condition to the entire source, which is always closed. No compactness or Hausdorff hypothesis is involved. In particular, this also covers an empty source, whose empty range is closed, without assuming the map continuous or onto. [Semmes §1.4; Prop.2.7.9](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L572).

Convergence to a given point is equivalent to convergence of its image under an embedding, because the domain has exactly the inherited target topology. The formal statement handles arbitrary filters, so it covers nets and sequences without a countability assumption. No Hausdorff condition or uniqueness of the limit is asserted. [Semmes §1.5; §2.7.1–2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L243).

An injective map becomes an embedding when its domain is equipped with the topology pulled back from the target. That particular domain topology is implicit in the displayed signature but explicit in the source. Injectivity then identifies it with the usual subspace topology on the range, with no continuity assumption needed beforehand. [Semmes Def.1.5.1; Prop.1.5.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L194).

A map is a homeomorphism exactly when it is continuous and has a continuous two-sided inverse. The two inverse identities give both injectivity and surjectivity; continuity is required in both directions. This matches the standard definition without compactness or separation hypotheses, and works for empty spaces when such inverse maps exist. [Semmes Def.2.8.2](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Homeomorph/Lemmas.lean#L502).

For a continuous injective open map, a closed source set equals the inverse image of the closure of its image. Openness and continuity let closure commute with inverse image; injectivity recovers the original set before closing it. The image itself may acquire extra ambient boundary points outside the map’s range. [Semmes §1.4.1; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L458).

An open map sends interior points of a set into the interior of its image: the image of the source interior is itself open and lies inside that image. The statement is an inclusion, allowing additional interior points in the image. Continuity and injectivity are unnecessary for this elementary openness consequence. [Semmes Def.1.4.9; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L401).

If g induces the topology on its domain, a map f into that domain is continuous at x exactly when g after f is continuous there. The equivalence follows by testing inverse images of target neighborhoods. Injectivity of g is unnecessary, and the statement imposes no openness or surjectivity requirement. [Semmes §2.7; Prop.2.8.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Basic.lean#L121).

Casting an integer quotient into a division ring preserves division when the denominator divides the numerator exactly and remains nonzero after casting. Both signs are allowed: exact divisibility removes rounding. The target nonzero condition also excludes denominators that vanish in positive characteristic; merely requiring a nonzero integer denominator would be insufficient. Compared with [Judson §§2.2,16.2](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Cast/Field.lean#L39).

Dividing by a positive natural number and then taking integer floor agrees with first taking floor and then using integer division. This holds for negative inputs too, because a positive integer divisor uses downward rounding. The theorem also includes denominator zero: Lean defines both field and integer division by zero as zero. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.7,8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Ring.lean#L295).

Every integer corresponds uniquely to its quotient and remainder on division by a positive natural n. The remainder lies between zero and n−1; the inverse sends (q,r) to qn+r. Negative inputs use floor division, so −1 at n=3 gives (−1,2). The nonzero assumption on n excludes an empty remainder range. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Logic/Equiv/Fin/Basic.lean#L372).

The fractional part is defined as a minus its integer floor, with that floor cast back into the ambient ring. On the reals this gives a value in [0,1), including for negative inputs: the fractional part of −3/2 is 1/2. The definition itself only supplies the subtraction formula, without extra order-compatibility assumptions. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Defs.lean#L264).

The fractional part a−floor(a) is nonnegative because floor(a) is no larger than a. This covers negative inputs as well as positive ones; it uses downward integer rounding, not truncation toward zero. The theorem explicitly assumes that addition preserves order, and integer inputs give equality rather than strict positivity. Compared with [Aspnes §4.7](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Floor/Ring.lean#L438).

Dividing two integers by their positive greatest common divisor produces coprime integers. The gcd is a natural number and is cast to an integer before division; both divisions are exact, so signs cause no rounding problem. Positivity excludes the pair (0,0), while allowing either input alone to be zero. Compared with [Aspnes §8.2](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/GCD.lean#L187).

Replacing an integer by its remainder on division by another integer preserves their greatest common divisor. This Euclidean step works because subtracting a multiple does not change common divisors. Signed inputs are allowed and the gcd is nonnegative. At divisor zero, the remainder is the original integer, so the equality still holds. Compared with [Aspnes §8.2.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Basic.lean#L89).

Replacing an integer divisor by its absolute value leaves the Euclidean remainder unchanged. For every nonzero divisor, the remainder is nonnegative and strictly below its absolute value, regardless of the divisor’s sign. At divisor zero both sides equal the dividend. Quotient rounding depends on the divisor’s sign; the remainder does not. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Group/Unbundled/Int.lean#L102).

Every integer has remainder zero or one on division by two. This is the usual even–odd split, including negative integers: −1 has remainder one, since the remainder is chosen nonnegative. The fixed positive divisor two guarantees that no division-by-zero convention is involved, and the two possible residues are distinct. Compared with [Aspnes §§8.1,8.4](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Init.lean#L276).

An integer square has residue zero modulo four when the integer is even, and residue one when it is odd. Lean expresses both cases by equating b² modulo four with b modulo two. The equality concerns ordinary nonnegative remainders, so it covers negative integers and excludes square residues two and three. Compared with [Aspnes §8.4.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Ring/Int/Parity.lean#L137).

For an even integer, dividing by two and multiplying back by two recovers the integer exactly. Integer division would normally round downward here, but evenness guarantees a zero remainder. Negative even integers and zero are included. The evenness hypothesis is substantive: for −3, the same expression gives −4 rather than −3. Compared with [Aspnes §§8.1,8.4](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Int/Even.lean#L78).

For an even natural number, dividing by two and multiplying by two returns the original number. Natural division takes the floor of the ordinary quotient, and evenness makes that quotient exact. Zero is included. The hypothesis cannot be dropped: for three, division gives one and multiplication back gives two. Compared with [Aspnes §§8.1,8.4](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Nat/Even.lean#L73).

If c divides a, dividing a+b by c equals the sum of the two natural quotients. The exact quotient of a prevents an extra carry from the remainders; b need not be divisible by c. Denominator zero is included under Lean’s convention that every natural quotient by zero is zero. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/ModEq.lean#L544).

Dividing two natural numbers by a common divisor preserves and reflects divisibility between them. Both divisions are exact, so rounding cannot change the comparison. A nonzero divisor is unnecessary here: if the common divisor is zero, the hypotheses force both numbers to be zero, and both divisibility statements are true. Compared with [Aspnes §8.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/GCD/Basic.lean#L277).

Two integers are congruent modulo n exactly when n divides their difference b−a. This is ordinary integer subtraction, so no ordering of a and b is needed. Negative moduli give the same congruence as their absolute values. Modulus zero is also covered: both sides then say that a equals b. Compared with [Aspnes §8.4.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/ModEq.lean#L106).

An integer is congruent to zero modulo n precisely when n divides it. The statement allows negative integers and negative moduli; Euclidean remainders are still nonnegative for nonzero moduli. At n=0 it reduces to a=0, because remainder modulo zero is the original integer and zero divides only zero. Compared with [Aspnes §8.4.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/ModEq.lean#L97).

For natural numbers with a≤b, congruence modulo n is equivalent to n dividing b−a. The ordering hypothesis prevents natural subtraction from stopping at zero and losing the difference. Without it, a=2, b=1, n=2 would incorrectly satisfy the divisibility condition. Modulus zero remains valid and reduces to equality. Compared with [Aspnes §8.4.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/ModEq.lean#L118).

A natural number is congruent to zero modulo n exactly when it is divisible by n. For positive n, this says its Euclidean remainder vanishes. The statement also handles n=0: remainder modulo zero is the original number, so congruence to zero and divisibility by zero both require that number to be zero. Compared with [Aspnes §8.4](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/ModEq.lean#L103).

Congruence modulo both m and n is equivalent to congruence modulo their least common multiple. Coprimality is unnecessary because the modulus is the lcm, not the product. Lean takes the lcm as a nonnegative natural number and casts it back to an integer; signed moduli and zero moduli are included. Compared with [Aspnes §§8.2,8.4](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/ModEq.lean#L357).

A natural number is odd exactly when its remainder modulo four is one or three. Reducing either of those residues modulo two gives one; conversely, the only odd residues among zero, one, two and three are one and three. Zero and all even natural numbers are correctly excluded. Compared with [Aspnes §8.4](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/ModEq.lean#L598).
